Nonreal quaternions $\qa,\qb$ are called similar if there exists a nonzero quaternion $\qp$ such that $\qp[][-1]\qa\qp = \qb$.
Let $\qa$ be a nonzero quaternion. Then, $\qq[][2] - \qa = 0$ has the solutions

issues.failure_explanation: When the two observations are parallel, $\ima[1]\times\ima[2]=0$ (and then also $\imb[1]\times\imb[2]=0$, since pairwise similarity forces $|\ima[1]\times\ima[2]|=|\imb[1]\times\imb[2]|$), the second alignment $\qq^{-1}(\ima[1]\times\ima[2])\qq=\imb[1]\times\imb[2]$ is vacuous and the true solution set is the full set of first-factor solutions. But the radicand $\qq_1^{-1}(\ima[1]\times\ima[2])\qq_1(\imb[2]\times\imb[1])$ is then $0$, so the stated formula gives $\qq_2=\lambda_2\sqrt{0}=0$ and hence $\qq=0$, which is not an admissible nonzero solution; no nonzero solution is represented. The proof derives the formula by applying the Sylvester solution theorem to $(\qa_3,\qb_3)=(0,0)$, but that theorem is stated for similar (hence nonreal) quaternions and the square-root lemma requires a nonzero radicand, so the invocation is outside its hypotheses. Example: $\qa_1=\qi,\qa_2=2\qi,\qb_1=\qj,\qb_2=2\qj$ are pairwise similar with a nonempty solution set, yet the formula yields only $\qq_2=0$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the missing degenerate case to the theorem: if $\ima[1]\times\ima[2]=0$ (equivalently $\imb[1]\times\imb[2]=0$), the second alignment is vacuous and the general solution is $\qq=\qq_1\qq_2$ with $\qq_1$ any nonzero solution of $\qa_1\qq_1=\qq_1\qb_1$ and $\qq_2$ an arbitrary nonzero quaternion commuting with $\qb_1$; the existing formula is unchanged otherwise.
issues.overall_effect: In the parallel-observation case the main theorem's general solution consists only of the inadmissible $\qq=0$, so the closed-form characterization of the zero-cost solution set is wrong (empty) in this case; the abstract's claim (ii) of a parameterization of all zero-cost quaternions is correspondingly affected.
issues.title: Second-factor formula collapses to zero for parallel observations, omitting all nonzero solutions
issues.why_classification: The formula fails completely in an explicitly attainable configuration (parallel observations) because the radicand vanishes and the invoked theorems' hypotheses (nonreal, nonzero) fail; recognizing this and supplying the correct centralizer description of $\qq_2$ is a contained case addition using the commutation constraint already derived in the proof, with no loss of the theorem's scope or closed form.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: In the degenerate case replace the side condition $\imq_2\perp\qa_3$ by the commutation-enforcing condition $\imq_2\parallel\qb_1$ (equivalently $\imq_2\times\qb_1=0$); justify dropping the $\lambda_2$ terms by showing $\qa_3\qb_3^*$ commutes with $\qb_1$ and that the chosen root lies in the centralizer of $\qb_1$ (or is real), which fails only in the corrected case; add the short missing sufficiency verification that every admissible pair $(\qq_1,\qq_2)$ satisfies both alignments; also replace $\qq_1^*$ by $\qq_1^{-1}$ in the formula, as the proof's definition of $\qa_3$ requires.
issues.overall_effect: In the degenerate case $\qq_1^{-1}(\ima_1\times\ima_2)\qq_1=-\imb_1\times\imb_2\neq0$ the stated solution set contains quaternions that do not solve the Wahba equation, and the claim that the parameterization is the general solution lacks a sufficiency proof even where the set is correct; the abstract's and conclusion's claims of a complete closed-form characterization are unreliable until repaired.

issues.why_classification: The printed solution set is mathematically wrong (overcomplete) in the degenerate case and the proof omits the sufficiency direction; repairing requires a new constraint analysis of which Sylvester solutions commute with $\qb_1$ plus a short verification argument, but it is contained and preserves the theorem's closed form, quantifiers, and scope, so it is more than minor yet short of serious.

Let $\qq[1]$ be a nonzero quaternion such that $\Abs{\qq[1][-1]\qa[1]\qq[1] - \qb[1]}^2 = 0$. Then, it equivalently holds $\qa[1]\qq[1] = \qq[1]\qb[1]$.

issues.failure_explanation: The first and third equalities silently identify $\qa_3=\qq_1^{-1}(\qa_1\times\qa_2)\qq_1$ with $\qq^{-1}(\qa_1\times\qa_2)\qq$; these differ in general. Since $\qq$ solves both alignments, $\qq^{-1}(\qa_1\times\qa_2)\qq=\qb_3$, so the display effectively asserts $\qa_3\qb_1=\qb_3\qb_1$, i.e. $\qa_3=\qb_3$, which need not hold. Counterexample: $\qa_1=\qb_1=\qi$, $\qa_2=\qb_2=\qj$, the solution $\qq=1$ with $\qq_1=\qi$ gives $\qa_3=-\qk$, and the display reads $(-\qk)\qi=\qk\,qi$, i.e. $-\qj=\qj$. The intended conclusion $\qa_3\qb_1=-\qb_1\qa_3$ is correct and follows by conjugating $(\qa_1\times\qa_2)\qa_1=-\qa_1(\qa_1\times\qa_2)$ with $\qq_1$ using $\qb_1=\qq_1^{-1}\qa_1\qq_1$; the repair is the forced substitution $\qq\to\qq_1$ in the display.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace $\qq$ by $\qq_1$ in the display so it reads $\qa_3\qb_1=\qq_1^{-1}(\qa_1\times\qa_2)\qa_1\qq_1=-\qq_1^{-1}\qa_1(\qa_1\times\qa_2)\qq_1=-\qb_1\qa_3$, using $\qb_1=\qq_1^{-1}\qa_1\qq_1$ instead of $\qb_1=\qq^{-1}\qa_1\qq$.
issues.overall_effect: One proof step of the main theorem is false as displayed; its conclusion is nevertheless correct and is used validly in the final computation ($2\mu_2(\qa_3+\qb_3)\qb_1$), so no downstream result is invalidated once the display is corrected.
issues.title: Displayed identity eq:B3_ORTHOGONAL_B1 conflates qq with qq1 and is false as written
issues.why_classification: A single forced symbol correction repairs the invalid inference; the intended conclusion is true and the later argument using it is valid, so every substantive claim survives a local, routine fix.
